newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Albania's exiled king says premier will have to go.
newsitem.headline: Albania's exiled king says premier will have to go.

text.p: Albania's exiled King Leka predicted on Wednesday that civil unrest in the Balkan country would force the resignation of the prime minister within 24 hours, and announced he was ready to step in.

Leka Zogu, who aspires to reinstate the monarchy founded by his father King Zog in 1928, called on Albanians to press for the government's resignation over the failed pyramid savings schemes which have beggared hundreds of thousands of investors.
In an interview in his home near Johannesburg, Leka said he saw the civil revolt as a sign it was time to position himself for a possible takeover, but ruled out armed insurrection.
"All the reports that I am getting from Albania at this moment are that the only person they have any interest in is myself," the 57-year-old Leka told Reuters.
"We expect Prime Minister Meksi to resign sometime today or tomorrow. All the parties with the exception of the Democratic Party are now demanding a referendum."
Leka said he was inundated with faxes and telephone calls from his native land.
Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi this week proposed deploying the army to quell rioting but has appeared to back away from the plan to use emergency rule.
Leka said Albanians in contact with him did not trust the government. In a message to his homeland, he said:
"My brothers and sisters... Make your demands through peaceful demonstrations. Ask for your rights and demand the resignation of this present government."
An exceptionally tall man with crew-cut grey hair, Leka wore a holstered pistol at his side throughout the interview. His South African home is protected by armed guards and five friendly Boxer dogs.
The chain-smoking pretender likes to be called "Your Majesty", and says his ambition is to fulfill his birthright by working to build up Albania's economy.

"It's a terrible situation and in fact it's a nightmare. The other nightmare is corruption...no sane person will gladly take it on. Unfortunately for me, I was born to it and duty is duty. I cannot stand by and see my people suffer."
Asked if he was planning to position himself closer to Albania, possibly on its borders, he replied:

"You probably know I do a lot of travelling and I do have forward bases from which I do operate. It depends entirely on developments that take place over the next few hours -- that is something that only God will know.
"I went into Albania in 1993 with even less possibilities," he said, referring to an ill-fated effort to return to the land he left when he was only three days old.

Leka was bundled back onto a private aircraft within 24 hours of touching down in Albania in November 1993. He had last seen the country in April 1939, when his father King Zog fled from occupying Italian troops under Benito Mussolini.
Political analysts in Tirana say there are two monarchist parties in Albania which do not seem to have great influence. But on the other hand people do not seem overtly hostile to Leka.
He said on Wednesday he would not take his 14-year-son, Prince Leka, his mother Geraldina or his wife Suzana to Albania.

"At this stage, until the situation in Albania has been clarified a bit and brought under control, I think it would be endangering them without any real gain to anyone...If anything should happen to me, he (the prince) is the heir-apparent to the throne."
He repeated his call for a referendum of Albania's 3.4 million people to decide if they wanted to remain under a republic or restore the monarchy.

"Any move on my side without the full backing of the people would be just as useless. That's why a referendum is so important because it would give the world and most importantly the Albanian people the right to have chosen for themselves.
"I am not interested in an armed insurrection."
